items.passage: Hippopotamuses spend much of the day submerged, but they also rest on riverbanks, exposing thick, nearly hairless skin to strong tropical sun. Within minutes of being secreted, the fluid that coats this skin, colorless at first, turns red and then brown; isolating the pigments responsible, chemist Yoko Saikawa and colleagues identified two unexpectedly acidic compounds, one red and one orange. Both compounds absorbed ultraviolet light and inhibited the growth of bacteria, suggesting that the secretion may function as both a sunscreen and an antibiotic.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It summarizes research that traced a color change in an animal’s skin secretion to particular pigments and showed that the change occurs only in strong sunlight.
It describes research that traced the color change in an animal’s skin secretion to two pigments and suggests that the color may signal to other animals.
It summarizes research that identified the compounds behind a color change in an animal’s skin secretion and that suggests the secretion may serve two protective purposes.
It summarizes research on the pigments in an animal’s skin secretion and suggests that the secretion protects the animal mainly while it is submerged.
items.explanation: The text explains that the fluid on a hippo’s skin turns from colorless to red to brown, reports that Saikawa’s team identified the red and orange compounds responsible, and notes that the compounds absorb ultraviolet light and slow bacterial growth, so the secretion may protect the skin in two ways. Choice C covers both parts: the compounds behind the color change and the hedged suggestion of a double protective role.

A.recipe: first part true, later part invented (INV)
A.why_wrong: The researchers did trace the color change to particular pigments, but the text says the change happens within minutes of the fluid being secreted; it never ties the change to strong sunlight.

B.recipe: first part true, later part invented (INV)
B.why_wrong: The researchers did trace the color change to two pigments, but the text says nothing about signaling; it links the pigments to sunscreen and antibiotic effects.

D.recipe: first part true, later part reversed (REV)
D.why_wrong: The text does suggest that the secretion is protective, but its sunscreen role matters when the hippo rests on riverbanks in strong sun; the text never says the protection works mainly underwater.

sources.what: Saikawa et al. (2004, Nature), hippo sweat turns from colorless to red to brown within minutes; red and orange pigments are unexpectedly acidic and have antibiotic and sunscreen activity

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal chemistry). Key C. Key parts: 2 (compounds behind the color change; may serve two protective purposes, hedged as the text hedges with 'suggesting' and 'may'). Hard rule: A true first part (pigments traced) fails on 'only in strong sunlight'; B true first part (color change traced to two pigments) fails on an invented signaling role; D true first part (research on the pigments, a protective secretion) fails on 'mainly while it is submerged', which the sunscreen role rules out (B and D rewritten in review: the old B was killed by 'inhibited', the old D was wholly off). Grazing left out of the passage because hippos graze mainly at night. The paper calls the fluid 'sweat'; the passage says 'fluid' and 'secretion' since it is neither sweat nor blood in the usual sense. Wikipedia (Hippopotamus) confirms the UV absorption and the antibacterial effect.

fixes: rewrote B (old B, 'encourages the growth of bacteria', was killed by 'inhibited'): now a true first part (color change traced to two pigments) failing on an invented signaling role
rewrote D (old D, an argument about why hippos stay submerged, was wholly off): now a protective-secretion reading that fails on 'mainly while it is submerged'

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Joseph Addison’s 1711 essay in The Spectator. Sir Roger de Coverley, a wealthy country gentleman, is the narrator’s friend.

As Sir Roger is landlord to the whole congregation, he keeps them in very good order, and will suffer nobody to sleep in [church] besides himself; for, if by chance he has been surprised into a short nap at sermon, upon recovering out of it he stands up and looks about him, and if he sees anybody else nodding, either wakes them himself, or sends his servants to them.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It describes a man who keeps order in church and explains how he came to be the landlord of the entire congregation.
It describes how a landlord’s authority over his tenants allows him to keep order in church and suggests that the tenants resent his watchfulness.
It recounts a particular Sunday on which a man woke from a nap during the sermon and then roused others who were sleeping.
It portrays a character who holds others to a standard of behavior that he himself does not always meet.
items.explanation: Sir Roger keeps the congregation “in very good order” and will let nobody sleep in church “besides himself”: whenever he wakes from one of his own naps, he looks around and wakes anyone else who is nodding, or has his servants do it. The text therefore portrays a man who holds others to a standard of behavior (staying awake during the sermon) that he himself does not always meet, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: Sir Roger does keep order in church, and the text says he is landlord to the whole congregation, but it never explains how he came to be their landlord; that position is simply what lets him keep them in order.

B.why_wrong: The text does link Sir Roger’s authority as landlord to the order he keeps in church, but it says nothing about how his tenants feel about being watched or woken.

C.why_wrong: The text does describe Sir Roger waking from a nap and rousing other sleepers, but it presents this as what he does whenever it happens (“if by chance he has been surprised into a short nap”), not as an account of one particular Sunday.

sources.what: The Spectator No. 112 (Monday, July 9, 1711), signed L. (Addison’s mark), text of the church paragraph

items.notes: Literary (1711 periodical essay, signed L., which the edition's introduction identifies as Addison's mark). Adapted: 'in it' replaced by '[church]' since the antecedent sentence is cut; otherwise copied exactly from the Gutenberg De Coverley Papers text. Key D, the shortest option (19 words), as in the band-7 model b0f7541b; reworded in review so it no longer echoes 'besides himself'. Hard rule: each wrong option keeps true content (keeps order and is landlord; authority as landlord lets him keep order; wakes from a nap and rouses sleepers) and fails on one later link (how he became landlord; tenants' resentment; one particular Sunday, where the text describes a habit). Review replaced the old A (shame), B ('entirely' his servants, killed by one phrase) and C (tenants reluctant to attend).
band7_moves: very short abstract key for an archaic narrative, as in b0f7541b ('It presents an account of a misunderstanding')
the deciding words ('besides himself' and 'surprised into a short nap') sit inside one long periodic sentence and must be decoded
every distractor keeps a true first half about Sir Roger's authority and fails on one later link (an invented feeling, an overreach on 'entirely', an invented effect on the tenants)

fixes: key D reworded more abstractly ('holds others to a standard of behavior that he himself does not always meet') so it no longer echoes 'besides himself'

rewrote A (shame, an inner state a reader could half-defend from his looking about), B ('entirely' his servants, killed by 'either wakes them himself') and C (tenants reluctant to attend): now how he became landlord, tenants' resentment, and one particular Sunday where the text describes a habit
explanation, why_wrong and notes updated; excerpt checked exact against Gutenberg De Coverley Papers, No. 112 (July 9, 1711) signed L. (Addison)

items.passage: As Britain’s colonies gained independence in the mid-twentieth century, colonial officials destroyed some sensitive records and secretly shipped others to Britain rather than handing them to the new governments. The existence of these “migrated archives” was officially acknowledged only in 2011, when Kenyans seeking compensation for abuses committed during the Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s forced their disclosure. The collection—<u>about 20,000 files from 41 former colonies</u>—had sat in government storage near London for decades before being opened to researchers at the National Archives in 2012 and 2013.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It conveys the size of a collection that, as the text explains, had been kept out of public view for decades.
It indicates how large the collection was in order to suggest that colonial officials destroyed far fewer records than they shipped to Britain.
It gives the size of the collection in order to explain why the government took so long to make the files public.
It details the extent of the collection and implies that historians had long suspected that such files existed.
items.explanation: The text says the migrated archives were secretly shipped to Britain, kept in storage for decades, and acknowledged only in 2011. The underlined portion tells how big that hidden collection was, about 20,000 files from 41 former colonies, which underscores the scale of what had been kept out of public view. Choice A names both the portion’s role (the size of the collection) and what the text says about that collection.

B.why_wrong: The portion does show how large the shipped collection was, but the text gives no figure for the records officials destroyed, so it makes no comparison between the two.

C.recipe: first part true, invented causal link (INV)
C.why_wrong: The portion gives the collection’s size, but the text does not use size to explain the long delay; it presents the files as having been kept secret until a lawsuit forced their disclosure.

D.why_wrong: The portion does detail the extent of the collection, but the text says nothing about what historians suspected before 2011.

sources.what: FCO migrated archives: about 20,000 files from 41 colonial dependencies, held clandestinely for decades in and around London, existence admitted in 2011 during the Mau Mau litigation, opened at TNA (FCO 141) in 2012 and 2013; some related material destroyed during decolonisation

items.notes: Area: history (archives, decolonisation). Key A. Modeled on 3.12 (an underlined figure that underscores extent). Key parts: 2 (size of the collection; kept out of view for decades). Hard rule: each wrong option opens with a true account of the portion (size, how large, extent) and fails on a later link (a comparison with the destroyed records; explains the delay; historians' suspicions). Review replaced the old B ('mostly Kenya'), which the underlined '41 former colonies' itself ruled out.

fixes: rewrote B (old B, 'most of the files concerned the uprising in Kenya', was ruled out by '41 former colonies' in the underline itself): now an invented comparison with the destroyed records

items.passage: Vietnamese American artist Dinh Q. Lê, who fled Vietnam with his family as a child and settled in Los Angeles, is celebrated for an unusual photographic technique. After completing a degree in photography, Lê began slicing photographs into strips and interweaving them, adapting a method of grass-mat weaving that his aunt had demonstrated during his childhood. Because the technique interlaces images so that each partially obscures another, it is well matched to Lê’s exploration of how personal memories of the Vietnam War intersect and conflict with Hollywood’s cinematic depictions of it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain where an artist’s distinctive technique came from and how it changed after he returned to live in Vietnam
To introduce an artist and his distinctive technique and suggest why that technique suits the subjects he explores
To describe an artist’s technique and argue that it owes more to his photography training than to his aunt’s weaving
To introduce an artist known for his photography and compare his methods with those of other artists who weave
items.explanation: The text introduces Dinh Q. Lê and his background, describes his method of weaving strips of photographs, which he adapted from grass-mat weaving, and then says the technique suited his exploration of how personal memories of the Vietnam War and Hollywood’s depictions of it intersect and conflict. Choice B covers all three parts: the artist, his technique, and why the technique fits his subject.

A.recipe: first part true, later part invented (INV)
A.why_wrong: The text does explain where the technique came from (his aunt’s grass-mat weaving), but it never mentions a return to Vietnam or any change in the technique.

C.why_wrong: The text does describe Lê’s technique, but it does not weigh his photography degree against his aunt’s grass-mat weaving; it says simply that he adapted her method after finishing his degree.

D.why_wrong: Lê is introduced as a photographer, but the text discusses no other artists, so it compares nothing.

sources.what: Dinh Q. Lê: born 1968 in Hà Tiên, fled in 1978, settled in Los Angeles; BFA in photography (UC Santa Barbara); photo-weaving inspired by his aunt's grass-mat weaving; series such as From Hollywood to Vietnam explore pop culture, personal memory and the gap between history and its media portrayals

items.passage: Popular-science writing often attributes expert performance in fields such as music and chess mainly to one factor: the total amount of deliberate practice—structured activity designed specifically to improve performance—that a person has undertaken. To evaluate this view, psychologists Brooke Macnamara, David Hambrick, and Frederick Oswald combined the results of dozens of earlier studies in a 2014 meta-analysis. Deliberate practice mattered, they found, but it accounted for only a modest proportion of the variation in performance in games, music, and sports, a smaller proportion in education, and almost none in professional work.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It reports the results of a review of earlier research to suggest that a popular explanation for expert performance has been overstated.
It presents the findings of a review of earlier research in order to argue that popular-science writers have misunderstood what deliberate practice involves.
It describes an analysis of research on expert performance in order to explain why practice tends to help people more in some fields than in others.
It discusses an analysis of research on expert performance and questions the methods used in the studies on which that analysis drew.
items.explanation: The text opens with a common view, that expert performance comes mainly from deliberate practice, and then reports a meta-analysis finding that practice mattered but explained only a modest proportion of the variation in performance in most fields and almost none in professions. Choice A captures this: the study is presented to show that the popular explanation claims more than the evidence supports.

B.why_wrong: The text does present the review’s findings, but what it questions is how much deliberate practice explains, not what the activity involves; the text simply defines the term and never says writers have defined it wrongly.

C.why_wrong: The text reports that practice accounted for more of the differences in some fields than others, but it offers no explanation of why.

D.why_wrong: The analysis is discussed, but the text never criticizes the methods of the earlier studies; it simply reports what combining them showed.

sources.what: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014, Psychological Science), meta-analysis: deliberate practice explained 26% of variance for games, 21% music, 18% sports, 4% education, under 1% professions; important but not as important as argued in popular-science writing

items.notes: Area: social science (psychology of expertise). Key A. Exact percentages left out (a 2018 corrigendum adjusted some figures); 'modest share', 'smaller share' and 'almost none' follow the abstract's ranking. Key parts: 2 (reports a review; suggests a popular explanation is overstated). Hard rule: B true first part fails on what is misunderstood (the definition of deliberate practice rather than its weight; rewritten in review, since the old 'no real difference' was killed by 'mattered'); C true first part fails on an invented explanation; D true first part fails on a methods critique.

fixes: rewrote B (old B, 'no real difference', was killed by 'mattered'): now the right review with the wrong target (writers misunderstood what deliberate practice is, not how much it explains)

items.passage: In the years following World War II, the progress of developing countries was conventionally evaluated by growth in national income. Pakistani economist Mahbub ul Haq, a former chief economist of Pakistan’s Planning Commission, came to see this yardstick as inadequate, arguing that development should be measured not only by economic gains but also by improvements in people’s well-being. As an adviser to the United Nations Development Programme, Haq launched its annual Human Development Report in 1990, which ranks countries by an index combining life expectancy and schooling with income.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text summarizes an economist’s objection to a standard measure of national progress and then explains why many of his colleagues rejected the alternative he proposed.
The text describes an economist’s doubts about how development was assessed and then traces how those doubts led Pakistan to change its economic policies.
The text outlines a criticism of a widely used economic yardstick and then argues that the measure it inspired has since replaced that yardstick.
The text presents an economist’s critique of a common way of gauging development and then describes a measure he introduced to address that shortcoming.
items.explanation: The first two sentences present Haq’s critique: judging development by income growth alone leaves out people’s well-being. The last sentence describes his response, the Human Development Report and its index combining life expectancy, schooling, and income. Choice D gives both moves in order.

A.recipe: first move right, second move invented (INV)
A.why_wrong: The text does summarize Haq’s objection, but it says nothing about colleagues rejecting his alternative.

B.recipe: first move right, second move invented (INV)
B.why_wrong: Haq’s doubts are described, but the text does not trace any change in Pakistan’s policies; it moves to his work at the United Nations.

C.recipe: first move right, second move invented (INV)
C.why_wrong: The text outlines the criticism and describes the index Haq introduced, but it makes no claim about how widely the index has been adopted or whether it has replaced income growth as the standard; it simply describes what the index measures.

sources.what: Human Development Report devised and launched by Mahbub ul Haq in 1990 to shift development economics from national income accounting to people-centred policies; HDI combines life expectancy, education and per capita income
Mahbub ul Haq: chief economist of Pakistan's Planning Commission in the 1960s, special adviser to UNDP from 1989

items.passage: Many birds can sense Earth’s magnetic field, but the receptor cells responsible have proved remarkably hard to find. <u>Earlier studies had identified iron-containing structures in the upper beaks of homing pigeons as nerve endings that formed a magnetic sensor</u>, a conclusion on which biologists and physicists alike came to rely heavily. In 2012, however, Christoph Treiber, David Keays, and colleagues systematically mapped these cells, finding that their number and location varied considerably from bird to bird—and that they were macrophages, a type of immune cell, rather than neurons.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It reports a claim about where a sensory ability originates that the text goes on to say was rejected after researchers found similar structures in birds that cannot sense magnetism.
It describes a widely accepted account of how pigeons sense magnetism that the text goes on to say was undermined by a closer study of the cells in question.
It presents a proposal about the anatomy of a sensory system that the text indicates was overturned, leading researchers to conclude that the sense depends on immune cells instead.
It identifies an influential finding about a group of cells that the text suggests was called into question because the original researchers had examined too few birds.
items.explanation: The underlined portion reports an earlier conclusion that iron-containing structures in pigeons’ beaks were nerve endings forming a magnetic sensor, a conclusion many researchers relied on. The next sentence says a 2012 study mapped those cells and found that they varied from bird to bird and were immune cells, not neurons. So the portion sets up a widely accepted account that a closer look at the cells undermined, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The portion does report a claim about the source of pigeons’ magnetic sense, and the text does say the claim was undermined, but not because of birds that lack the sense; the 2012 team found that the cells varied from bird to bird and were immune cells, not neurons.

C.why_wrong: The text does indicate that the proposal was overturned, but it never says the immune cells produce the magnetic sense; it opens by noting that the receptor cells responsible have proved hard to find, and nothing suggests the macrophages detect magnetic fields.

D.why_wrong: The finding was influential and was called into question, but not because too few birds were examined; the 2012 team found that the cells varied from bird to bird and were immune cells.

sources.what: Treiber et al. (2012, Nature): earlier studies claimed magnetite-containing trigeminal afferents in the pigeon upper beak, widely accepted and relied upon by behavioural biologists and physicists; iron-rich cells are macrophages, not magnetosensitive neurons, and vary in number and distribution

items.notes: Area: natural science (sensory biology). Key B. Key parts: 2 (a widely accepted account; undermined by a closer study of the cells). Section 6 checks: key 29 words; options 27 to 30 words; all three distractors keep a true first part and fail only in the later clause (review rewrote A, which said 'confirmed', and C, which said pigeons cannot detect magnetic fields: both were killed by one stated fact); the span is a set-up (a view the next sentence overturns), not the main claim; the deciding sentence comes after the span. Treiber is first author and Keays senior author of the 2012 paper.
band7_moves: the span is a view that a later sentence overturns, and the key carries both halves (as in 1f2d6173 and a2f64e58)

all three distractors keep a true paraphrase of the span and change only the outcome: confirmed (REV), pigeons cannot sense fields (overreach), too few birds (invented cause that echoes 'varied considerably from bird to bird')
abstract key with no passage nouns beyond 'pigeons'; the student must read past the span to the 2012 study to answer

fixes: rewrote A (old A said the claim was 'confirmed', the reverse of the next sentence): now the claim rejected for an invented reason (birds that cannot sense magnetism)
rewrote C (old C said pigeons cannot detect magnetic fields, contradicted by the first sentence): now an invented conclusion that the sense depends on immune cells

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Yung Wing’s 1909 memoir My Life in China and America.

All through my college course, especially in the closing year, the lamentable condition of China was before my mind constantly and weighed on my spirits. In my despondency, I often wished I had never been educated, as education had unmistakably enlarged my mental and moral horizon, and revealed to me responsibilities which the sealed eye of ignorance can never see, and sufferings and wrongs of humanity to which an uncultivated and callous nature can never be made sensitive. But this is a low view of life, a cowardly feeling and unworthy of a being bearing the impress of divinity.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why the narrator chose to attend college in the United States rather than in China
To show that the narrator’s education made him less concerned about the problems facing his home country
To convey how the narrator’s awareness of China’s troubles led him to a wish that he came to regard as unworthy
To describe the narrator’s regret about the particular subjects he chose to study during his years at an American college
items.explanation: The narrator says China’s “lamentable condition” weighed on him throughout college, so that he often wished he had never been educated, since education had made him see responsibilities and sufferings that ignorance cannot see. He then calls that wish “a low view of life, a cowardly feeling and unworthy.” Choice C captures both the distress and his rejection of the wish it produced.

A.why_wrong: The text never says why the narrator attended college in the United States; it describes his feelings while he was there.

B.why_wrong: Education made the narrator more sensitive to “sufferings and wrongs,” not less concerned; China’s condition “weighed on [his] spirits.”

D.why_wrong: The narrator’s regret is a passing wish that he had not been educated at all, not regret about particular subjects, which the text never mentions.

sources.what: Yung Wing, My Life in China and America (Henry Holt, 1909), chapter V, text of the passage (one sentence omitted, hence 'adapted')
Yung Wing graduated from Yale College in 1854

items.notes: Literary (1909 memoir; copyright page reads 'Published November, 1909'). Adapted: the sentence 'The more one knows, the more he suffers ...' between the second and third sentences is omitted; the rest is copied exactly. Key C. Distractor mix for medium P_lit: INV, REV, INV.

items.passage: Many flowers reward their pollinators with nectar, but the South African plant Ceropegia sandersonii offers its visitors nothing at all; its principal pollinators are tiny Desmometopa flies, which ordinarily feed on the bodies of honeybees captured by spiders. Biologist Annemarie Heiduk and her colleagues discovered that the plant exploits this feeding habit: <u>its flowers emit a scent closely resembling the chemicals that honeybees release when they are attacked</u>. Lured by the scent, the flies crawl into the flowers, which temporarily trap them, and they pick up pollen before escaping.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It explains how the plant attracts the insects that pollinate it.
It identifies the reason that the flies feed on honeybees.
It describes how spiders locate the honeybees they capture.
It contrasts the plant’s scent with the scents of flowers that offer nectar.
items.explanation: The text says the plant offers its pollinators no reward and that the flies normally feed on honeybees caught by spiders. The underlined portion explains how the plant takes advantage of this: its scent imitates the chemicals released by honeybees under attack, which draws the flies in. So the portion explains how the plant attracts its pollinators.

B.why_wrong: The text says the flies feed on honeybees caught by spiders, but the underlined portion is about the flower’s scent, not why the flies eat honeybees.

C.why_wrong: Spiders are mentioned only as the animals that catch honeybees; nothing in the text explains how they find their prey.

D.why_wrong: The text mentions nectar-producing flowers in its first sentence, but the underlined portion describes this plant’s scent without comparing it with theirs.

items.passage: Because large whales spend most of their lives submerged and are difficult to approach safely, monitoring their health presents considerable challenges. To investigate the microbes inhabiting the airways of humpback whales, marine microbiologist Amy Apprill and her colleagues adopted an unconventional approach. <u>They maneuvered a small six-rotor drone through the cloud of droplets that a whale exhales upon surfacing, collecting the spray on sterile plates and dishes mounted on the drone.</u> Samples from whales off Massachusetts and British Columbia shared a core community of bacteria, a finding that could help scientists track the health of whale populations.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It explains why whales exhale clouds of droplets when they surface.
It presents an unexpected finding about the bacteria in whales’ airways.
It identifies a problem with earlier methods of studying large whales.
It describes how the researchers obtained the samples they analyzed.
items.explanation: The text says that whales are hard to approach and monitor and that Apprill’s team adopted an unconventional approach. The underlined sentence describes that approach: a drone flew through a whale’s exhaled spray and caught droplets on sterile plates and dishes. The next sentence reports what the samples showed. So the underlined sentence describes how the researchers got their samples.

A.why_wrong: The sentence mentions the cloud a whale exhales, but it does not explain why whales produce it.

B.why_wrong: The finding about a shared core community of bacteria comes in the following sentence; the underlined sentence describes how samples were collected.

C.why_wrong: The first sentence notes why whales are hard to monitor; the underlined sentence describes the researchers’ own method rather than faulting earlier ones.

sources.what: Apprill et al. (2017, mSystems): small unmanned hexacopter collected exhaled blow from humpback whales off Cape Cod and Vancouver Island on sterile PCR plates and petri dishes; 25 core bacteria common to all whales; framework for health monitoring

items.notes: Area: natural science (marine microbiology). Key D. Method span as in 2.20. Cape Cod and Vancouver Island given as Massachusetts and British Columbia.

items.passage: Why does the reflective layer at the back of a reindeer’s eye change color with the seasons? Like many mammals, reindeer possess a tapetum lucidum, a mirrorlike tissue behind the retina; in Arctic reindeer, however, this tissue is golden in summer but deep blue in winter. Researchers Karl-Arne Stokkan, Glen Jeffery, and colleagues propose an explanation: during the prolonged winter darkness, permanently dilated pupils probably increase pressure inside the eye, compressing the tissue’s collagen fibers so that it reflects shorter, bluer wavelengths. Instead of returning light directly out of the eye, the blue tissue scatters more of it through the retina, enhancing sensitivity at some cost to visual sharpness.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text asks why a trait of an animal changes over the year, then explains why researchers have been unable to answer that question.
The text asks why a trait of an animal changes over the year, then presents an explanation that a team of researchers has proposed.
The text describes a trait that many mammals share, then argues that reindeer are the only mammals that lack it.
The text compares the eyes of two kinds of animals, then describes how those animals find food in the dark.
items.explanation: The text opens with a question about why the reflective layer in a reindeer’s eye changes color with the seasons. The rest of the text gives the explanation that Stokkan, Jeffery, and colleagues propose: in winter, pressure inside the eye compresses the tissue so that it reflects bluer light and scatters more light through the retina, making the eye more sensitive in the dark. Choice B describes this question-then-answer structure.

A.recipe: first move right, later move reversed (REV)
A.why_wrong: The text does ask why the trait changes, but it then presents the researchers’ proposed answer rather than saying they could not find one.

C.recipe: first move partly right, later move reversed (REV)
C.why_wrong: The text says reindeer, like many mammals, have a tapetum lucidum; it never claims they lack it.

D.why_wrong: The text discusses only reindeer and says nothing about how they find food.

sources.what: Stokkan et al. (2013, Proc. R. Soc. B): reindeer tapetum lucidum golden in summer, deep blue in winter; raised intraocular pressure probably from permanent pupil dilation compresses collagen; blue reflection scatters light through photoreceptors, increasing sensitivity at the cost of acuity

items.notes: Area: natural science (vision). Key B. 'Probably' kept from the paper's hedge on the cause of the pressure.

items.passage: William Henry Fox Talbot’s The Pencil of Nature (1844), the first commercially published book illustrated with photographs, is celebrated as a milestone in the history of photography. But eight months before Talbot’s book appeared, botanist Anna Atkins had begun issuing Photographs of British Algae, a book of cyanotype prints of dried seaweed. Atkins’s privately published volume came first, and she deserves to be remembered as a pioneer of the photographic book.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain how Talbot developed the printing process that Atkins later used to make the images in her book
To compare the quality of the images in two early books of photographs
To argue that Atkins deserves recognition for a book that came before a more celebrated one
To describe the kinds of seaweed that Atkins collected along the coast of Britain
items.explanation: The text notes that Talbot’s 1844 book is celebrated as a milestone, then points out that Atkins began issuing her book of cyanotypes eight months earlier and concludes that she “deserves to be remembered as a pioneer.” The text therefore argues that Atkins should be recognized for a book that preceded Talbot’s better-known one.

A.why_wrong: The text never says who developed the cyanotype process, and it does not credit Talbot with Atkins’s method.

B.why_wrong: The text compares the two books’ dates, not the quality of their images.

D.why_wrong: Seaweed is mentioned only as the material Atkins printed; the text does not describe kinds of seaweed or where she found them.

sources.what: Anna Atkins self-published the first installment of Photographs of British Algae: Cyanotype Impressions in October 1843, considered the first book illustrated with photographic images; Talbot's The Pencil of Nature followed eight months later (June 1844) as the first commercially published one; cyanotypes made by placing dried algae directly on the paper
The Pencil of Nature (1844): first commercially published book illustrated with photographs, regarded as an important and influential work in the history of photography

items.notes: Area: humanities (history of photography). Key C. Explicit argument with an evaluative close ('deserves to be remembered'), as in 2.18. The cyanotype process (Herschel, 1842) is left unnamed so distractor A fails on the text alone.

items.passage:
The following text is from Booth Tarkington’s 1914 book Penrod. Penrod, a boy of eleven, dreads playing the Child Sir Lancelot in a pageant.

There was no escape; and at last his hour was hard upon him. Therefore he brooded on the fence and gazed with envy at his wistful Duke.

<u>The dog’s name was undescriptive of his person</u>, which was obviously the result of a singular series of mesalliances [mismatched pairings]. He wore a grizzled moustache and indefinite whiskers; he was small and shabby, and looked like an old postman. Penrod envied Duke because he was sure Duke would never be compelled to be a Child Sir Lancelot.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It introduces a mismatch that the description of the dog in the following sentence illustrates.
It offers a reason for the envy that Penrod is described as feeling in the sentence just before it.
It establishes that Penrod chose the dog’s name himself.
It contrasts the dog’s appearance with Penrod’s appearance.
items.explanation: The underlined portion says that the dog’s grand name, Duke, does not describe him. The following sentence shows why: he is small and shabby, with a grizzled moustache, and looks like an old postman. So the portion sets up a mismatch between name and appearance that the next sentence illustrates.

B.why_wrong: Penrod’s envy is explained in the last sentence (Duke will never have to play Sir Lancelot), not by the underlined portion, which is about the dog’s name and looks.

C.why_wrong: The text never says who named the dog.

D.why_wrong: The text describes only the dog’s appearance; Penrod’s appearance is never mentioned.

items.passage:
The following text is from Willa Cather’s 1915 novel The Song of the Lark. Harsanyi, a piano teacher in Chicago, has recently begun giving lessons to Thea Kronborg, a young woman from a small town in Colorado.

The best thing about her preparation was that she had developed an unusual power of work. He noticed at once her way of charging at difficulties. She ran to meet them <u>as if they were foes she had long been seeking</u>, seized them <u>as if they were destined for her and she for them</u>. Whatever she did well, she took for granted.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portions in the text as a whole?
options: To suggest that Thea regards her teacher as a rival whom she hopes to defeat
To indicate that Thea hopes to avoid the difficulties she meets in her lessons
To reveal Thea’s belief that she is fated to become a famous pianist
To emphasize the eagerness with which Thea takes on challenges in her work
items.explanation: Harsanyi notices Thea’s “way of charging at difficulties.” The underlined portions compare the difficulties to foes she has long been seeking and to things destined for her, so she runs to meet them and seizes them. These images emphasize how eagerly she takes on challenges.

A.why_wrong: The “foes” are the difficulties in her work, not her teacher; nothing suggests she sees Harsanyi as a rival.

B.why_wrong: Thea runs to meet difficulties and seizes them; she does not try to avoid them.

C.why_wrong: “Destined” refers to the difficulties being meant for her; the text says nothing about fame.

items.notes: Literary (1915 novel). Copied exactly; the excerpt starts mid-paragraph at a sentence boundary and stops before 'Her eagerness aroused ...', which would state the key. Thea comes from Moonstone, Colorado; Harsanyi teaches in Chicago. Two underlined portions, plural stem as in 2.23.

items.passage: In Pedagogy of the Oppressed (1968), Brazilian educator Paulo Freire criticized what he called the “banking” model of education, in which teachers deposit knowledge into passive students as if filling empty containers; instead, he argued, learners should help create knowledge through dialogue. Freire’s ideas shaped the work of his fellow Brazilian Augusto Boal, who in the 1970s developed what he called the Theatre of the Oppressed. In Forum Theatre, one of its best-known forms, audience members may stop a short scene depicting an injustice and step onstage to act out their own solutions, becoming what Boal called “spect-actors.”
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text describes a disagreement between an educator and a theater director, then explains how the two resolved it.
The text outlines an educator’s view of how people learn best, then describes a form of theater shaped by that view.
The text outlines an educator’s view of how people learn best, then explains why theater artists later rejected that view.
The text traces the history of theater in Brazil, then lists the techniques that its directors most often use.
items.explanation: The first sentence presents Freire’s view that learners should help create knowledge through dialogue rather than passively receive it. The rest of the text describes Boal’s Theatre of the Oppressed, which Freire’s ideas shaped and in which audience members step onstage to act out solutions. Choice B describes this idea-then-influenced-work structure.

A.why_wrong: Freire and Boal are not presented as disagreeing; Freire’s ideas shaped Boal’s work.

C.recipe: first move right, later move reversed (REV)
C.why_wrong: The text does outline Freire’s view, but it then shows a theater artist building on that view, not rejecting it.

D.why_wrong: The text discusses one theater practice influenced by one educator, not the history of Brazilian theater or its directors’ usual techniques.

sources.what: Theatre of the Oppressed: theatrical forms Augusto Boal elaborated in the 1970s, influenced by Paulo Freire's Pedagogy of the Oppressed; Forum Theatre lets spectators stop a scene and come onstage as spect-actors to act out an intervention
Pedagogy of the Oppressed, first published 1968; Freire calls traditional pedagogy the banking model and argues the learner should be a co-creator of knowledge

items.notes: Area: humanities (education and theater). Key B.

items.passage:
The following text is from Lord Byron’s 1809 poem English Bards and Scotch Reviewers. Fitzgerald was a minor poet of the time.

Still must I hear?—shall hoarse Fitzgerald bawl
His creaking couplets in a tavern hall,
And I not sing, lest, haply [perhaps], Scotch Reviews [Scottish literary journals]
Should dub me scribbler, and denounce my Muse?
Prepare for rhyme—I’ll publish, right or wrong:
Fools are my theme, let Satire be my song.
Oh! Nature’s noblest gift—my grey goose-quill!
Slave of my thoughts, obedient to my will,
Torn from thy parent bird to form a pen,
That mighty instrument of little men!
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The speaker complains that audiences prefer another poet’s work to his own, then resolves to imitate that poet’s popular style.
The speaker admits that critics were right to call him a scribbler, then promises to write more carefully in the future.
The speaker refuses to let the threat of harsh reviews keep him silent, then declares the kind of poetry he means to write.
The speaker recalls how he first learned to write poetry, then thanks the friend who gave him his first pen.
items.explanation: The speaker first asks whether he must stay silent, out of fear that Scottish reviewers will call him a scribbler, while a poor poet like Fitzgerald keeps performing. He answers by announcing, “I’ll publish, right or wrong,” names satire of fools as his theme, and calls on his pen for the task. Choice C gives both moves.

A.why_wrong: The speaker mocks Fitzgerald’s “creaking couplets”; he says nothing about audiences preferring Fitzgerald and has no wish to imitate him.

B.why_wrong: The speaker does not concede that the reviewers are right; he refuses to be silenced by them and will publish “right or wrong.”

D.why_wrong: The goose-quill is the pen he will write with, praised as “Nature’s noblest gift”; the poem mentions no lessons and no friend who gave him a pen.

sources.what: English Bards, and Scotch Reviewers, lines 1-10, Works of Lord Byron (ed. Coleridge), vol. 1

items.notes: Literary (1809 satire; Byron wrote it after the Edinburgh Review mocked his first collection). Lines 1-10 copied exactly from the Coleridge edition; two bracketed glosses added. The excerpt stops at the end of a sentence ('little men!'). Key C.

The following text is from Sarah Orne Jewett’s 1890 novel Betty Leicester. Fifteen-year-old Betty, visiting her elderly grandaunts for the summer, has just been escorted to an unfamiliar bedroom for the night.

It was a solemn, big, best bedroom, with dark India-silk curtains to the bed and windows, and dull coverings on the furniture. <u>This all looked as if there were pretty figures and touches of gay color by daylight, but now by the light of the two candles on the dressing-table it seemed a dim and dismal place that night.</u> Betty was not a bit afraid; she only felt lonely.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It suggests that Betty is frightened of spending the night alone in the room.
It explains why Betty decides to ask her aunts for a different room.
It shows that Betty admires the expensive silk curtains in the room.
It emphasizes how gloomy the bedroom seems to Betty at night.
items.explanation: The first sentence describes the dark curtains and dull coverings of the bedroom. The underlined sentence adds that, although the room might look cheerful by daylight, by candlelight it seems “a dim and dismal place.” It emphasizes how gloomy the room appears to Betty at night, which fits the loneliness mentioned in the last sentence.

A.why_wrong: The text says directly that “Betty was not a bit afraid; she only felt lonely.”

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text says Betty asks for another room.

C.why_wrong: The silk curtains are mentioned as dark, and the underlined sentence stresses how dismal the room looks, not Betty’s admiration for anything in it.

items.passage:
The following text is from Myrtle Reed’s 1910 novel Master of the Vineyard. Rosemary, a twenty-five-year-old woman, has climbed a hill overlooking her village.

From the top of the hill she surveyed her little world. Where the small white houses clustered in the valley, far below her, she had spent her five-and-twenty years, <u>shut in by the hills, and, more surely, by the iron bars of circumstance</u>. To her the heights had always meant escape, for in the upper air and in solitude she found detachment—a sort of heavenly perspective upon the affairs of the common day.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It conveys Rosemary’s sense that her life in the valley has confined her.
It indicates that the windows of Rosemary’s house are covered with iron bars.
It suggests that Rosemary has only recently moved to the valley.
It shows that Rosemary is afraid of climbing the steep hills around her village.
items.explanation: The underlined portion says Rosemary has been “shut in” by the hills and, even more, by “the iron bars of circumstance.” The image of a prison conveys that she feels confined by the life she has led in the valley, which is why, as the next sentence says, the heights mean escape to her.

B.why_wrong: The “iron bars” are a figure for her circumstances; the text never describes her house or its windows.

C.why_wrong: The text says she has spent all her “five-and-twenty years” in the valley.

D.why_wrong: Rosemary has climbed the hill, and the heights mean escape to her; nothing suggests she fears climbing.

items.passage: Educator and athlete Lucy Diggs Slowe accumulated a remarkable series of firsts. While studying at Howard University in Washington, DC, she was among the founders of Alpha Kappa Alpha, the first sorority established by African American women, in 1908. In 1917 she captured the women’s championship at the American Tennis Association’s inaugural national tournament, becoming the first African American woman to win a major athletic title. In 1922 Howard appointed her its first dean of women, a position she occupied until her death in 1937.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain how Slowe first became interested in playing tennis
To present several achievements of a pioneering educator and athlete
To compare Slowe’s work as a teacher with her work as a dean
To argue that more universities should appoint deans of women
items.explanation: The text opens by saying Slowe “accumulated a remarkable series of firsts” and then lists three of them: helping found the first sorority established by African American women, winning the first American Tennis Association women’s title, and becoming Howard’s first dean of women. Its purpose is to present her achievements.

A.why_wrong: The text reports Slowe’s tennis title but never says how she became interested in the sport.

C.why_wrong: The text does not mention her teaching or compare it with her work as a dean.

D.why_wrong: The text describes Slowe’s appointment as dean of women but makes no recommendation to other universities.

The following text is from L. M. Montgomery’s 1910 novel Kilmeny of the Orchard. Eric Marshall, a recent college graduate temporarily teaching at a rural school, discovers an old orchard during an evening walk.

The charm of the place took sudden possession of Eric as nothing had ever done before. He was not given to romantic fancies; but the orchard laid hold of him subtly and drew him to itself, and he was never to be quite his own man again. He went into it over one of the broken panels of fence, and so, unknowing, went forward to meet all that life held for him.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why Eric decides to repair the orchard’s broken fence
To show that Eric often daydreams about places he has never visited
To convey the powerful effect that a place has on Eric
To describe Eric’s worry about entering land that belongs to a stranger
items.explanation: The text says the orchard’s charm “took sudden possession” of Eric “as nothing had ever done before,” that it “laid hold of him” and drew him in, and that he was “never to be quite his own man again.” Its main purpose is to convey how strongly the place affects him.

A.why_wrong: Eric climbs over a broken panel of the fence to enter the orchard; nothing suggests he plans to repair it.

B.why_wrong: The text says Eric “was not given to romantic fancies,” which is why the orchard’s effect on him is so striking.

D.why_wrong: Eric is drawn into the orchard and walks in; the text says nothing about worry or about who owns the land.

items.passage: Nnenna Okore is a sculptor who grew up in Nsukka, a university town in southeastern Nigeria, and now teaches art in Chicago. Her mostly abstract works are built from humble or discarded materials such as burlap, wire, and paper, and more recently from food scraps that she turns into bioplastic. Okore shapes these materials through slow, repetitive processes—weaving, sewing, rolling, twisting, and dyeing—that she learned in part by watching people in Nigeria carry out everyday household tasks.

options: It describes a traditional Nigerian craft, then lists several artists who have adapted it.
It presents a debate about the use of recycled materials in art, then gives one artist’s view.
It compares the sculptures of two artists, then explains why one of them is better known.
It introduces an artist, then describes the materials and methods she uses in her work.

The rest of the text describes her work: the humble or discarded materials she uses and the slow processes, such as weaving and twisting, by which she shapes them. Choice D describes this structure.

items.passage: Researchers have documented numerous animals that appear to medicate themselves with plants. It explains why great apes in Africa use medicinal plants.
It describes how researchers analyzed the leaves in a laboratory.
It argues that orangutans use plants more skillfully than other apes do.

items.passage: Insects flourish almost everywhere on land and in freshwater habitats, but they are remarkably scarce in the sea. It is therefore tempting to conclude that the open ocean is the one environment insects never colonized. That conclusion, however, overlooks the sea skaters. These small, wingless relatives of pond water striders glide across the water’s surface, capturing small prey, and five species of these Halobates insects spend their entire lives on the open ocean, far from any coastline.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why most insects are unable to survive in salt water
To argue that the open ocean is not entirely free of insects
To compare sea skaters with the water striders that live in ponds
To describe how storms carry insects from the coast out to sea
items.explanation: The text grants that insects are scarce in the sea and that it is tempting to think none live on the open ocean. It then says this conclusion “overlooks the sea skaters,” five species of which spend their whole lives far from any coastline. The text argues that the open ocean is not completely free of insects.

A.why_wrong: The text says insects are scarce in the sea but never explains why.

C.why_wrong: Pond water striders are mentioned only as relatives of sea skaters; the two are not compared.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about storms; it describes sea skaters that live on the open ocean all their lives.

items.passage: During the 1880s, several African American women obtained US patents for inventions intended to simplify household and workplace tasks, although biographical information about some of them is scarce. Goode, who operated a furniture store in Chicago, patented a bed that folded into a cabinet. And in 1888, Miriam E. Benjamin, a schoolteacher, patented a hotel chair equipped with a signal that allowed guests to summon assistance.

The text summarizes a debate among historians, then gives reasons for supporting one side of that debate.
The text makes a general observation about a group of inventors, then gives specific cases that illustrate it.
The text describes one inventor’s career, then compares her with inventors from other countries.

The rest of the text gives three specific cases, Reed’s dough kneader, Goode’s cabinet bed, and Benjamin’s signal chair. Choice C describes this structure.

B.why_wrong: The text presents no debate among historians.

items.passage: Fluorescence—absorbing light of one color and emitting it as another—is well documented in many marine organisms, including corals and jellyfish. <u>Among four-limbed animals, however, it had been reported mainly in parrots and sea turtles</u>, so a 2017 discovery by Carlos Taboada and colleagues was unexpected: under ultraviolet illumination, the South American polka-dot tree frog glows a brilliant blue-green. The researchers traced this glow to a previously unknown family of fluorescent compounds in the frog’s skin and lymph, which they named hyloins.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It defines a term that is used throughout the rest of the text.
